hints: Focus on working backwards, addition polymers form when the C=C double bond opens to make single bonds in a long chain.
Look at one repeating pair in polymer W, one carbon has two Cl atoms and the next carbon has one Cl and one methyl group.
Join that two-carbon pair back together with a double bond to get the monomer, then count the longest chain containing the double bond to name it.
walkthrough:
**Recall how addition polymerisation works**

Think of polymerisation as unzipping a C=C double bond. Each monomer contributes two backbone carbons joined by a single bond in the polymer.

To find the monomer, reverse this. Pick out one two-carbon unit from the chain and put the double bond back.

**Identify the repeat unit in W**

Look carefully at the section. The backbone alternates.

$$-\text{CCl}_2 - \text{CCl}(\text{CH}_3)-$$ 
One carbon carries two $\text{Cl}$ atoms. The neighbour carries one $\text{Cl}$ and one $\text{CH}_3$ group. This two-carbon pattern repeats over and over.

**Rebuild monomer V**

Close the single bond between those two carbons back into a double bond:
$$\text{CCl}_2 = \text{CCl}(\text{CH}_3)$$
This molecule has 3 carbons in total, with 3 $\text{Cl}$ atoms and one double bond.

**Name the monomer correctly**

The longest chain containing the C=C has 3 carbons, so the parent is propene. Number from the double bond end to give lowest locants.
$$\text{CCl}_2 = \text{CCl} - \text{CH}_3$$
This is 1,1,2-trichloropropene.

options.A: Incorrect. Butene means a 4-carbon parent chain. Monomer V has only 3 carbons (two backbone carbons plus one methyl carbon). A butene monomer would give an extra $\text{CH}_2$ group in the polymer backbone.
options.B: Incorrect. 1,1,2-trichloroethene is $\text{CCl}_2 = \text{CHCl}$. It has only 2 carbons and no methyl group. The polymer in the diagram clearly shows a $\text{CH}_3$ branch on every second backbone carbon, so ethene is too short.
options.C: Correct. Reversing the polymer gives $\text{CCl}_2 = \text{CCl}(\text{CH}_3)$. The longest 3-carbon chain with the double bond is propene, with two Cl on C1 and one Cl on C2, giving 1,1,2-trichloropropene.
options.D: Incorrect. This draws the same connectivity as C, $\text{CCl}_2 = \text{C}(\text{Cl})(\text{CH}_3)$, but the name is wrong. IUPAC requires the longest chain containing the double bond as the parent. That is 3 carbons, so it must be called a substituted propene, not a substituted ethene.
